title: Nested loops, hash join and merge join
description: Learn how SQL Server executes joins using nested loops, hash joins, and merge joins, and when each is chosen.

data.text: SQL Server supports three physical join algorithms: nested loops, hash join, and merge join. Each has different memory, CPU, and I/O characteristics. The optimizer chooses the algorithm based on estimated row counts, available indexes, and sort order of the inputs.

Nested loops is the simplest join algorithm. For each row in the outer input, SQL Server searches for matching rows in the inner input using an index seek or scan. It is usually the best choice when the outer input is small and the inner input has a supporting index.

data.title: Query favoring nested loops
data.content: When one table is small and the other has an index on the join column, the optimizer often chooses nested loops.
data.code:
SELECT o.OrderID, c.CustomerName
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2024-01-01';

data.text: Hash join is used when the inputs are large, the join column is not indexed, or the inputs are unsorted. SQL Server builds a hash table on the smaller input and probes it with the larger input. Hash joins are memory-intensive but can be very fast for large, unsorted data sets.

data.title: Hash join memory grants
data.text: If the hash table does not fit in memory, SQL Server spills it to tempdb. Spilling causes extra I/O and slows the query. You can see spills in the actual execution plan as warnings on the Hash Match operator.

Merge join requires both inputs to be sorted on the join column. If suitable indexes exist, SQL Server can read the inputs in order without an explicit sort. Merge join is linear and efficient, but it requires sorted inputs and is usually chosen only when the optimizer knows the data is already ordered.

cards.title: Nested loops
cards.description: Best for small outer inputs with indexed inner inputs.
cons: Poor when outer input is large
Many random I/Os if inner input lacks an index

cards.title: Hash join
cards.description: Best for large, unsorted, or non-indexed inputs.
pros: Scales well with large data sets
cons: Spills to tempdb if memory is insufficient

cards.title: Merge join
cards.description: Best when both inputs are already sorted on the join key.
pros: Linear cost relative to input size

data.title: Takeaway
points: Nested loops is best for small outer inputs with indexed inner inputs
Hash join handles large, unsorted data sets but needs memory
Merge join is efficient when inputs are already sorted
Index design directly affects which join algorithms are available
data.takeaway: The optimizer picks the join algorithm that matches the shape of your data and indexes. Tune indexes and statistics to give it better options.
